title: UK-India Free Trade Deal Opens Manchester's Door to Indian Manufacturers
excerpt: Indian firms are eyeing Manchester's advanced materials hub and lower operating costs as the bilateral trade agreement eliminates tariffs on machinery and opens access to 40,000 UK procurements.
body:
• The UK-India Free Trade Agreement, ratified in July 2025, includes immediate tariff cuts on advanced machinery and opens access to 40,000 UK government procurements for Indian businesses
  • Manchester has been voted the best-performing UK city outside London for foreign direct investment three times in five years
  • India is Greater Manchester's fastest-growing partner country for service exports, now worth £337 million annually
  • Indian companies including Tech Mahindra, HeroCycle, and Tata Steel already operate in Manchester, with new investments accelerating

A year after Britain and India ratified their landmark free trade agreement, Manchester is emerging as the primary gateway for Indian manufacturers seeking a foothold in the UK and European markets — offering a combination of world-class research infrastructure, lower costs, and direct air links to the subcontinent.

The Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, signed in May 2025 and ratified two months later during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to London, includes immediate tariff cuts on advanced machinery. For Indian manufacturers in sectors ranging from automotive components to aerospace, the deal has removed barriers that previously made UK expansion uneconomical.

Why Manchester, Not London

The numbers make the case plainly. Operating costs in Greater Manchester run up to 40 percent lower than London, according to Invest Manchester. The city boasts 180 specialist advanced materials firms, a 115,000-strong manufacturing workforce, and the largest graduate pipeline of any UK regional city.

Manchester has been voted the best-performing UK city outside London for attracting foreign direct investment three times in the last five years. India is now Greater Manchester's fastest-growing partner country for service exports, with trade worth £337 million to the local economy.

The city's research ecosystem is a particular draw. The University of Manchester, where graphene was first isolated, anchors a cluster of advanced materials research that has few global rivals. The Henry Royce Institute — the UK's national centre for advanced materials — recently signed a memorandum of understanding with Tata Steel, which is investing £10 million over four years in a Centre for Innovation in Manchester.

Infrastructure Catching Up

Connectivity has improved markedly. Manchester Airport now offers direct flights to Mumbai, Delhi, Singapore, and key Chinese cities. IndiGo launched Mumbai service four times weekly in July 2025, and strong demand has sustained the route.

The newly inaugurated Consulate General of India in Manchester, opened in March 2025, prioritises business engagement and regional cooperation — a signal of the diplomatic weight both governments are placing on the corridor.

The Trade Deal's Fine Print

The FTA's provisions go beyond tariff cuts. India has agreed to reduce levies on 90 percent of British products, with 85 percent becoming tariff-free within a decade. In return, 99 percent of Indian exports to Britain face no duties, according to the World Economic Forum. The deal includes a dedicated innovation chapter — reportedly the first in any Indian trade agreement — and provisions for cross-border data flows and paperless trade.

For manufacturers, the procurement provisions may prove most significant. Indian businesses now have a guaranteed right to compete for a share of the UK's 40,000 government procurements that meet specified criteria. Under the "Make in India" equivalence provision, UK-based Indian suppliers offering at least 20 percent domestic content qualify for preferential treatment previously reserved for Indian firms.

"This FTA gives our small businesses and workforce a much-needed global platform."

— Piyush Goyal, India's Commerce Minister

Indian Companies Already on the Ground

The pipeline is not theoretical. Tech Mahindra and HeroCycle already have operations in Manchester. Indian textile exports to the UK are projected to rise 30 to 45 percent by 2030, translating to an additional $500 to $800 million in annual export value, according to India's commerce ministry. Agricultural exports are expected to surge 20 percent within three years, with zero-duty access for 95 percent of agro-products including spices, cereals, and ready-to-eat meals.

On the import side, Indian consumers are benefiting from reduced tariffs on Scotch whisky — down from 150 to 75 percent immediately, declining to 40 percent over the next decade — and on automobiles, where duties have dropped from over 100 percent to 10 percent under a quota system.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 1.9 million people of Indian origin living in the UK — the country's largest ethnic minority — the trade agreement creates new professional opportunities in manufacturing, services, and trade facilitation. Manchester's growing Indian business community and institutional infrastructure make it an increasingly natural landing point for entrepreneurs and professionals looking to bridge the two economies.

The agreement also sets a template for future partnerships. As global supply chains diversify away from single-country dependence, the UK-India corridor — with Manchester as its industrial anchor — offers a model for how complementary economies can build shared capabilities rather than simply exchange goods.
